# Transferring Files

<!-- This file is generated by filen-cli. Do not edit it directly! -->

Files and directories are transferred between your computer and your Filen drive with
`upload` and `download`. Directories are always transferred recursively.

Like `cp`, both commands place the transferred item *inside* the destination when it is an
existing directory or ends in `/`, keeping its name: `upload ./notes /backups` creates
`/backups/notes`, and `download /backups/notes .` creates `./notes`. Any other destination is
the transferred item's new path: `upload ./notes.txt /backups/old.txt` uploads it as `old.txt`,
and `download /backups/notes ./old-notes` creates `./old-notes`. Missing directories on the way
to the destination are created, in the drive and locally. Downloading `/` writes the whole
drive's contents into the destination.

`upload` takes several local items, as in `upload *.jpg /photos`. Where no shell expands a
wildcard, on Windows, whose shells pass it on as it is, and in the REPL and commands piped into
the CLI on every platform, `upload` expands `*`, `?` and `[...]` in its local paths itself the
way a Unix shell does: each matches within one level of directories, and a name starting with
`.` only when the pattern does too (case-insensitively on Windows). A path that names an
existing item is uploaded as it is, even when it holds a `[`, and a path that matches nothing is
uploaded as it was given.

Uploading a file where the drive already holds a file of the same name replaces it: the upload
becomes the current file, and the one it replaced is kept as an earlier version when file
versioning is enabled for your account. Uploading a directory onto an existing one adds its
contents to it, replacing same-named files the same way. A downloaded file replaces a local
file at its path, except when the local file already has the same contents, which is then left
as it is. In a directory download, a local file of the same size is also left as it is when
the drive holds no hash of the file's contents and the local file is not older. Uploads keep
each file's modification and creation times, and downloads set the modification time on the
local file (and the creation time on macOS and Windows).

With `--skip-existing`, `upload` leaves out each file the drive already holds a file of the same
name for (the drive compares names case-insensitively), and with `--update` it leaves one out
unless its size differs or it was modified after the drive's copy. With `--no-clobber`,
`download` never replaces a local file. The files left out are counted in the result and listed
with `-v`, and so are the files a directory download leaves as they are for already holding
the same contents.

With `--resume`, a download that does not finish, for an error or for Ctrl+C, keeps what it
wrote of the file it was writing, beside the file's path in a temp file named after the
remote file (ending in `.filendl`), and the next `download --resume` of that file continues
from there instead of starting over. A file that was changed in the drive since is a new
version, which starts over. A continued file is checked against the hash of its contents that
the drive holds, when it holds one; when they differ, the kept part is removed and the
download fails, to start over next time. So is a file that was not continued and differs from
that hash: what it wrote is not kept. The bytes a download did not have to download again
count as transferred, and the result names them as resumed and leaves them out of the speed.
Without `--resume`, an unfinished file is removed.

With `--resume`, an upload that does not finish keeps an encrypted record of the chunks of the
file the drive acknowledged, in `uploads/` in the config directory, and the next
`upload --resume` of the same file to the same place continues it, for a single file and for
the files of an uploaded directory alike: the whole file is read again to check its hash, but
only what is missing is sent. A file that was changed since, or a record more than about a day
old, starts over. Files of 7 MiB or less are not recorded. The bytes an upload did not have to
send again count as transferred, and the result names them as resumed. The records are encrypted
with your account's keys, so only you can read them, and are removed once the upload finishes
or after a day. Without `--resume`, nothing is kept.

With `--include` and `--exclude`, a directory transfer takes only some of the items inside the
directory. Both take a gitignore-style pattern, can be given several times, and match the path
of an item relative to the transferred directory, case-insensitively: `*.jpg` matches every
JPEG file, `photos/` every directory named `photos`, and `docs/*.md` the Markdown files
directly inside `docs` at the top. With `--include`, only the files a pattern matches are
transferred, along with everything inside a directory a pattern matches and the directories on
the way to them; an excluded item is left out, a directory with everything inside it, even
where an include pattern matches it. A file named as the item to transfer is transferred
whatever the patterns say.

Like `cp`, both commands take several items at once, followed by a destination that is then
always a directory, created when missing: `upload a.txt b.txt ./photos /backups` uploads all
three into `/backups`. An item that fails is listed at the end while the others are still
transferred, and the result adds them all up. A shell expands a wildcard such as `*.jpg` into
such a list of items; the Windows command prompt does not, and remote paths take no wildcards.

`download` also takes the URL of a public link, as the web app or `public-link` gives it, to
download the file or directory it shares, even from another account:
`download 'https://app.filen.io/#/f/<uuid>%23<key>' ./shared`. Downloading only links needs no
login. A password-protected link takes its password from `--link-password` or the
`FILEN_CLI_LINK_PASSWORD` environment variable, or asks for it.

With `-` in place of the local path, `upload` reads stdin and `download` writes stdout, as in
`tar -cz notes | filen upload - /backups/notes.tar.gz` and
`filen download /backups/notes.tar.gz - | tar -xz`. The upload's destination then has to name
the remote file, and only a single file can be downloaded to stdout, which carries nothing but
the file: there is no progress line, and the result goes to stderr. `-` works only for a single
command, not in the REPL or among commands piped into the CLI, where stdin carries the commands.

An uploaded symlink is uploaded under its own name with the contents it points to. Inside an
uploaded directory, symlinks are followed the same way; with `--no-follow-symlinks` they are
skipped instead (neither the link nor what it points to is uploaded): listed with `-v`, counted
in the result without it, and listed in the `--json` result's `skipped_symlinks`.

While a transfer runs, its progress line shows the current speed and the time left, and the
result ends with the number of files and bytes transferred, the time taken and the average
speed. With `-v`, each file of a directory transfer is listed as it completes. The global
flags `--concurrency`, `--upload-bandwidth-kbps` and `--download-bandwidth-kbps` limit the
concurrent connections and cap the upload and download bandwidth, in kilobytes per second.

When a single item inside a directory transfer fails, the rest of the transfer still completes,
the failures are listed at the end, and the command exits with a nonzero status. With
`--json`, the result is printed as one object instead: `{"destination": ..., "files": ...,
"bytes": ..., "resumed_bytes": ..., "skipped": ..., "skipped_symlinks": [...], "failed":
[{"path": ..., "error": ...}]}`, where `path` is `null` for a failure not about a single item.
Press Ctrl+C to cancel a running transfer: what was transferred by then, and the items that had
failed, are reported on stderr and the command exits with status 130, where the TypeScript CLI
printed "Aborted".

> `upload [OPTIONS] <SOURCE> [PATH]...`  
> Upload a local file or directory (recursively) to the Filen drive  
> 🠊 `<SOURCE>` Local file or directory to upload, or "-" to upload stdin as the file the destination names  
> 🠊 `[PATH]...` More local files or directories to upload, followed by the destination: the directory in the Filen drive to upload into, or, after a single item, that item's new path when it is not an existing directory and does not end in "/"; missing directories are created (default: the current working directory)  
> 🠊 `--no-follow-symlinks` Skip the symlinks inside an uploaded directory instead of uploading what they point to (counted in the result, listed with -v)  
> 🠊 `--skip-existing` Skip each file the drive already holds a file of the same name for, instead of replacing it (listed with -v)  
> 🠊 `--update` Replace a file the drive already holds a file of the same name for only when its size differs or it was modified since, and skip it otherwise (listed with -v)  
> 🠊 `--resume` Keep a record of what was uploaded of a file when the upload does not finish, and continue from there when the file is uploaded again with --resume  
> 🠊 `--include <PATTERN>` Transfer only the files inside a directory that match this gitignore-style pattern, along with the directories on the way to them and everything inside a directory it matches (repeatable)  
> 🠊 `--exclude <PATTERN>` Leave out the items inside a directory that match this gitignore-style pattern, a directory with everything inside it, even where --include matches them (repeatable)

> `download [OPTIONS] <SOURCE> [PATH]...`  
> Download a file or directory (recursively) from the Filen drive  
> 🠊 `<SOURCE>` File or directory to download ("/" for the entire Filen drive), or the URL of a public link to download the file or directory it shares  
> 🠊 `[PATH]...` More files or directories to download, followed by the destination: the local directory to download into, or, after a single item, that item's new path when it is not an existing directory and does not end in a path separator; missing directories are created (default: the current local directory); "-" writes a single file to stdout  
> 🠊 `--no-clobber` Never replace a local file: skip each file whose local path is taken (listed with -v)  
> 🠊 `--resume` Keep what was downloaded of a file when the download does not finish, and continue from there when the file is downloaded again with --resume  
> 🠊 `--link-password <PASSWORD>` The password of a password-protected public link to download (asked for when needed and not given) [env: FILEN_CLI_LINK_PASSWORD]  
> 🠊 `--include <PATTERN>` Transfer only the files inside a directory that match this gitignore-style pattern, along with the directories on the way to them and everything inside a directory it matches (repeatable)  
> 🠊 `--exclude <PATTERN>` Leave out the items inside a directory that match this gitignore-style pattern, a directory with everything inside it, even where --include matches them (repeatable)

## Syncing

`sync` keeps local directories in sync with directories in your Filen drive. Each sync pair is a
local directory, a remote directory and a mode, which says which way changes go and whether
deletions do:

- `twoWay` (or `tw`), the default: what changes on either side is changed on the other,
  deletions included. A file changed on both sides since the last pass is a conflict, which the
  passes leave alone until it is resolved.
- `localToRemote` (or `localToCloud`, `ltc`): the remote directory mirrors the local one. What is
  created, changed, moved or deleted locally is done on the remote, and what only the remote has
  is deleted there. Nothing is downloaded.
- `remoteToLocal` (or `cloudToLocal`, `ctl`): the local directory mirrors the remote one, the
  other way round. Nothing is uploaded.
- `localBackup` (or `lb`): as `localToRemote`, but nothing is ever deleted on the remote: a file
  deleted locally stays on the remote. A path where the two sides hold a file and a directory is
  a conflict (see below).
- `remoteBackup` (or `cloudBackup`, `cb`): as `remoteToLocal`, but nothing is ever deleted
  locally. A path where the two sides hold a file and a directory is a conflict (see below).

Mode names are case-sensitive. A remote file or directory that a sync deletes goes to the trash
of your Filen drive; a local one goes to the sync pair's `.filen-sync-trash` (see below).

A sync pair is given as `<local>:<remote>` (two-way) or `<local>:<mode>:<remote>`, as an
argument or with `--pair`, or as a sync pairs file. The remote path is what follows the last
`:`, so a remote path with a `:` in it can only be given in a sync pairs file. `sync` without
sync pairs syncs the sync pairs of the default sync pairs file (see below); it does not sync the
sync pairs earlier runs set up and the sync database still holds, unless they are given again.

> `sync [OPTIONS] [PAIR]...`  
> Sync one or more sync pairs, continuously until Ctrl-C or once with --once  
> 🠊 `[PAIR]...` Pair of local and remote directories to sync. Format: `<local>:<remote>` (two-way) or `<local>:<mode>:<remote>`, where `<mode>` is one of `twoWay` (or `tw`), `localToRemote` (or `localToCloud`, `ltc`), `remoteToLocal` (or `cloudToLocal`, `ctl`), `localBackup` (or `lb`), `remoteBackup` (or `cloudBackup`, `cb`). The remote path is what follows the last `:`, so a remote path with a `:` in it can only be given in a sync pairs file. Alternatively, the path to a sync pairs file: YAML, or JSON as the TypeScript CLI's syncPairs.json. If none are given, the pairs of syncPairs.yaml in the config dir, or else of syncPairs.json there, or else, with the default config dir, of the TypeScript CLI's ~/.filen-cli/syncPairs.json. Or the alias a pair has (its `alias` key) in that default sync pairs file  
> 🠊 `-p, --pair <PAIR>` A sync pair, as a PAIR argument gives it  
> 🠊 `--once` Run one sync pass for each sync pair, then exit  
> 🠊 `--continuous` Keep syncing until Ctrl-C, which is what `sync` does without --once. Kept for compatibility with the TypeScript CLI  
> 🠊 `--dry-run` Print what a pass of each sync pair would do, and sync nothing. The sync pairs are registered as without it  
> 🠊 `--debounce-ms <MS>` How long, in milliseconds, a burst of changes must go quiet before a pass syncs it (1 to 60000; 800 by default). Applies to a continuous sync only  
> 🠊 `--safety-net-secs <SECS>` The fewest seconds between the full passes a continuous sync runs whatever has changed (1 to 86400; 300 by default). A sync pair whose full pass takes long waits longer. Applies to a continuous sync only  
> 🠊 `--approve-mass-deletions` Approve the deletions the delete guard holds back. Applies to every sync pair, in its first sync pass only  
> 🠊 `--keep-local <RELATIVE_PATH>` When a conflict occurs at the given path or under it, keep the local side. The path is relative to the root of each sync pair, and applies to every sync pair, in its first sync pass only  
> 🠊 `--keep-remote <RELATIVE_PATH>` When a conflict occurs at the given path or under it, keep the remote side. The path is relative to the root of each sync pair, and applies to every sync pair, in its first sync pass only  
> 🠊 `--keep-both <RELATIVE_PATH>` When a conflict occurs at the given path or under it, keep both sides. The path is relative to the root of each sync pair, and applies to every sync pair, in its first sync pass only

## Sync pairs files

A sync pairs file is YAML, or JSON as the TypeScript CLI's syncPairs.json was. It lists sync
pairs under `syncPairs`, or is a list of them, or is a single sync pair:

```yaml
syncPairs:
  - local: ~/Documents
    remote: /Documents
    mode: twoWay
    alias: docs
    ignore:
      - "*.tmp"
      - build/
    excludeDotFiles: true
  - local: photos
    remote: /Backups/Photos
    syncMode: localBackup
```

Each sync pair has:

- `local`: the local directory. A leading `~` is the home directory, and a relative path is
  relative to the file's directory.
- `remote`: the remote directory, which may contain a `:`.
- `mode`, or `syncMode` as the TypeScript CLI called it: a mode name or its short form, `twoWay`
  if not given. Giving both is an error.
- `alias`, optional: a word, without `:` or a path separator, by which `filen sync <alias>`
  selects the sync pair of the default sync pairs file, and by which the commands that manage
  sync pairs name it. A file that gives any other alias is refused.
- `ignore`, optional: a list of ignore rules, in `.filenignore` syntax, which are added to the
  `.filenignore` at the local root (see below).
- `excludeDotFiles: true`, optional: stands for the rules `.*` and `!/.filenignore`, so every
  dot file and dot directory is left out of the sync, but the `.filenignore` itself.
- `disableLocalTrash`, the TypeScript CLI's key, is read but only gives a warning, since the
  local trash cannot be turned off.

Any other key is an error.

`sync` without sync pairs reads syncPairs.yaml in the config directory, or else syncPairs.json
there. With the default config directory, it then falls back to `~/.filen-cli/syncPairs.json`,
where the TypeScript CLI kept its sync pairs when its install script had set it up; with
`--config-dir`, it does not look in the home directory. That file is also where an alias is
looked up.

## Running a sync

By default, `sync` keeps syncing until you press Ctrl+C: a change on either side is synced
shortly after it is made, and a full pass runs every few minutes as well. `--continuous` says
the same and is accepted for the TypeScript CLI's sake. With `--once`, it runs one sync pass for
each sync pair and exits when they are done.

A continuous sync waits until a burst of changes has gone quiet for 800 milliseconds before a
pass syncs it; `--debounce-ms` sets that wait. It also runs a full pass at least every 300
seconds, whatever has changed, to catch a change it was not told about; `--safety-net-secs`
sets that time. A sync pair whose full pass takes long waits longer between them: up to 6
hours, or the time given if that is longer. The safety net must be longer than the debounce.

The first Ctrl+C stops the sync once the passes in flight have finished. A second Ctrl+C quits
at once, without waiting for them, and exits with 130.

When the local or the remote directory of a sync pair does not exist, `sync` asks whether to
create it, and creates it with any missing directory above it; `--yes` answers yes. Without a
terminal to ask at and without `--yes`, the command fails instead. A local path that is a file
is an error. `sync` looks up every sync pair's directories, and asks about each missing one
once, before it creates any. A sync pair the sync database then refuses, such as one that
overlaps another, leaves behind the directories created for it.

`sync` says which sync pairs it starts on, then prints a line for each thing a pass does, with
the time and the sync pair; failures go to stderr. A path that fails the same way again on a
later pass is not named again: that pass's summary counts it. With `--quiet`, it prints only
failures, what needs attention or was settled, and what each pass did. Every line also goes to
the log files (unless `--no-log-file` is given), so a sync nobody watches leaves a record. When
stderr is a terminal, a line at its bottom shows what the running transfers have moved, redrawn
in place; `--quiet` leaves it out.

While it watches, `sync` also says when a sync pair's passes keep failing (and when they work
again), and when it cannot hear about local or remote changes as they happen, which the
periodic full pass then picks up instead. On Linux, a tree with more directories than
`fs.inotify.max_user_watches` allows is one cause. With `--json`, each change of a watch's
health is a `watch_status` object.

With `--json`, `sync` prints one JSON object per line for each event instead, such as
`{"pair":1,"label":"...","event":"uploaded","path":"a.txt"}`. A transfer's `progress` comes at
most once a second for each sync pair, with the bytes the pass has moved each way so far
(`pass_uploaded_bytes`, `pass_downloaded_bytes`), and `pass_completed` carries the pass's counts,
its conflicts, errors and unsyncable paths, and the bytes it moved. `uploaded` and `downloaded`
come once a file has landed; the other actions (`creating_remote_dir`, `trashing_remote`,
`deleting_local`, `moving_remote` and so on) as they start. What the flags settle is an
`approved` object with a `message`, and a conflict they could not resolve a `resolve_failed`
object with its `path` and a `message`. A `conflict` object carries its `reason` (`diverged`,
`remote_keeps_dir`, `remote_keeps_file`, `local_keeps_dir` or `local_keeps_file`) and the
`resolutions` that can resolve it (`keep_local`, `keep_remote`, `keep_both`). There is no
banner and no status line. A failed action, a failed pass and a refused pass are their objects
on stdout, like every other event, and nothing of them goes to stderr; failures that are not an
event's still go to stderr as text. `--json` takes precedence over `--quiet`: every event is
printed.

With `--dry-run`, `sync` prints what a pass of each sync pair would do: what it would transfer,
create, move or delete, the deletions the delete guard would hold back and why, the conflicts it
would leave and the paths it cannot sync. It syncs nothing, but sets the sync pairs up as `sync`
does: they are registered, and the ignore rules of their sync pairs file are added to their
`.filenignore`. It does not create a local or remote directory that does not exist. A paused
sync pair is not planned, as `sync` runs no pass of it: it says on stderr that the pair is
paused instead. With `--json`, it prints one `plan` object per sync pair it plans.

`sync --once` exits with 0 when the last pass of every sync pair completed and left nothing
undone: no errors, no held deletions, no conflicts and no paused sync pair. Otherwise it exits
with 1, after naming each sync pair and what it left. `sync` without `--once` exits with 0 when
Ctrl+C stops it and the last pass of every sync pair left nothing undone, and with 1 when a sync
pair could not be synced or its last pass left something. Ctrl+C exits `sync --once` with 130,
and a second Ctrl+C, which quits without waiting for the passes in flight, exits either with
130. An invalid command line, such as an unknown mode, exits with 2.

## Deletions, conflicts and the local trash

Before a pass deletes anything, the delete guard looks at what it would delete, and holds every
deletion of the pass back when:

- the local scan did not complete, as when a directory could not be read,
- the sync pair has not completed a pass yet, or tracks nothing yet, so that a first sync cannot
  wipe a destination that already holds files,
- the remote directory is listed as empty while the sync pair still tracks files in it, and the
  pass would delete more than one of them,
- or the pass would delete more than 10 items and more than half of the items the sync pair
  tracks.

The rest of the pass still runs. The held deletions are printed as needing attention, and wait
until they are approved; a missing mount or a fault on the server can look like a mass deletion,
so check before approving.

A conflict is a path changed on both sides since the last pass. The passes leave it alone until
it is resolved: by keeping the local version, which is uploaded, the remote version, which is
downloaded, or both, the local one being renamed aside to `<name>.old.<ext>` and synced as a file
of its own.

In `localBackup` and `remoteBackup`, a path where one side holds a file and the other a directory
is a conflict too, whichever side made them differ: the source changed the item's kind, another
client replaced the destination's, or a first sync met a destination that already held the other
kind. A backup never deletes on its destination, so the destination's item stays, and only what
moves the local item off the path resolves it: keeping both, which renames the local item to
`<name>.old.<ext>`, or, where the local item is a file, keeping the remote version, which moves
it into `.filen-sync-trash`. Renaming or moving either item yourself, or giving one side the
other's kind, makes it an ordinary conflict once a pass has seen that, which any `--keep-*` then
resolves. Keeping the local version cannot resolve it, nor can keeping the remote version over a
local directory: `sync` and `resolve-sync-conflict` refuse those, leave the conflict as it is and
say what would resolve it, and the question at the terminal offers only what does.

`--approve-mass-deletions` approves the deletions the delete guard holds back, and
`--keep-local`, `--keep-remote` and `--keep-both` resolve conflicts. A `--keep-*` path is
relative to the root of a sync pair, and covers the conflicts at that path and under it as a
directory: `dir` covers `dir/f`, while `a.txt` does not cover `a.txt.bak`. Where two paths cover
a conflict, the longer one decides, and `.` covers the whole sync pair. These flags apply to
every sync pair of the run, and only to what the first pass of each sync pair finds; a pass
that failed before it planned found nothing for them, so they also apply to the next one. A
flag that cannot resolve the conflict it covers is a failure for that path, which stays a
conflict; with `--once`, one more pass then applies what was settled before the command exits.
What a later pass holds back or finds in conflict is printed as needing attention, or asked
about.

What the flags leave is asked about at the terminal once the pass that found it has ended, when
stdout and stderr are terminals, there is a terminal to answer at (stdin, or the controlling
terminal), without `--json` and without `--no-input`: whether to
apply a held batch of deletions, listing up to 20 of them, and which version of a conflicting
file to keep, or neither for now. A batch or a conflict is asked about once while it lasts, and
what the flags settle is not asked about. The approval of deletions only lives in this
`filen sync`, so there is no command to give it later; a conflict can also be resolved later with
`resolve-sync-conflict`. `--yes` does not answer these questions. While a question is open,
`sync` keeps syncing and prints what happened once it is answered; Ctrl-C at the question
answers "not now", and a further Ctrl-C stops the sync. With `--once`, the questions come after
the passes, and one more pass applies what the answers settled.

A local file or directory that a sync deletes, or replaces with the remote's version, is not
destroyed but moved into `.filen-sync-trash` at the sync pair's local root, under the day it was
moved (`.filen-sync-trash/YYYY-MM-DD/<path>`), and deleted from there after 30 days. That
folder is never synced. The trash is always on, and there is no flag to turn it off.

## Ignoring files

A `.filenignore` file in any directory of a sync pair lists, in gitignore syntax, the files and
directories under it that are not synced.

Before a sync pair is synced, the rules of its sync pairs file that the `.filenignore`
at its local root lacks are added to the end of that file, which is created if there is none.
No line is ever removed: a rule taken out of the sync pairs file stays in `.filenignore` until
you remove it there. A mode that uploads (`twoWay`, `localToRemote`, `localBackup`) syncs that
`.filenignore` like any other file, so the rules apply on the remote side too; in a mode that
only downloads (`remoteToLocal`, `remoteBackup`), a `.filenignore` at the local root that was
never synced stays local and applies on top of the remote's. There is no `--ignore` flag:
ignore rules belong to a sync pair, in its `.filenignore` or its sync pairs file.

## The sync database

What each sync pair last synced is kept in the sync database, `sync-engine.db` in the config
directory. Sync pairs stay registered there after the run that set them up, so the next run
of the same sync pair only syncs what changed meanwhile. A run that cannot set up one of its
sync pairs registers none of them. Only one `filen sync`, or one of the commands that manage sync
pairs, can use that database at a time.

A sync pair the TypeScript CLI synced keeps what that CLI last synced: when `sync` sets up a
sync pair that has not finished a pass yet, it imports the state the TypeScript CLI kept for the
same `<local>:<remote>`, written as that CLI was given it, from `sync/state/v2` in that CLI's data
directory (the config directory, or `~/.filen-cli`), and says how many synced files it took
over. The first pass then takes a file that neither side has changed since for synced, instead
of weighing both copies as new.

## Managing sync pairs

The sync pairs `sync` has set up stay registered in the sync database, and these commands
manage them. They name a sync pair by the id `list-sync-pairs` prints, by its alias in the
default sync pairs file, or by its local directory. They open the same database as `sync`, so
they cannot run while a `filen sync` is running: stop it first.

A sync pair whose mode `set-sync-mode` changed must be given to `sync` in its new mode from then
on, in a sync pairs file too: `sync` refuses a sync pair given in another mode than the one it is
registered in, and says which one that is.

> `list-sync-pairs`  
> List the registered sync pairs

> `remove-sync-pair <PAIR>`  
> Remove a sync pair from the sync database; its files stay as they are on both sides  
> 🠊 `<PAIR>` The sync pair: its id, as list-sync-pairs prints it, its alias in the default sync pairs file, or its local directory

> `set-sync-mode [OPTIONS] <PAIR> <MODE>`  
> Change the mode of a sync pair, from its next pass on
>
> By default, what the destination still holds of what the source no longer has is kept: the switch deletes nothing, and in a one-way mode those copies stay on the destination. A switch from a backup mode to one that deletes would otherwise delete them.  
> 🠊 `<PAIR>` The sync pair: its id, as list-sync-pairs prints it, its alias in the default sync pairs file, or its local directory  
> 🠊 `<MODE>` The new mode: `twoWay` (or `tw`), `localToRemote` (or `localToCloud`, `ltc`), `remoteToLocal` (or `cloudToLocal`, `ctl`), `localBackup` (or `lb`), `remoteBackup` (or `cloudBackup`, `cb`)  
> 🠊 `--propagate-deletions` Let the next pass delete, on the destination, what the source no longer has, as the new mode says. The delete guard still holds a large batch of deletions back for approval

> `list-sync-conflicts <PAIR>`  
> List the conflicts a sync pair holds, which its passes leave alone: paths changed on both sides, or holding a file and a directory in a backup mode  
> 🠊 `<PAIR>` The sync pair: its id, as list-sync-pairs prints it, its alias in the default sync pairs file, or its local directory

> `resolve-sync-conflict <--keep-local|--keep-remote|--keep-both> <PAIR> <PATH>`  
> Resolve a conflict of a sync pair; the next pass of the sync pair applies it  
> 🠊 `<PAIR>` The sync pair: its id, as list-sync-pairs prints it, its alias in the default sync pairs file, or its local directory  
> 🠊 `<PATH>` The path of the conflict, relative to the root of the sync pair, as list-sync-conflicts prints it  
> 🠊 `--keep-local` Keep the local version, which the next pass uploads  
> 🠊 `--keep-remote` Keep the remote version, which the next pass downloads. A local version that differs is moved into the sync pair's .filen-sync-trash first  
> 🠊 `--keep-both` Keep both: the local version is renamed aside, to `<name>.old.<ext>`, and synced as a file of its own

> `retry-sync <PAIR> [PATH]`  
> Let the next pass of a sync pair try again the paths it stopped trying after they failed repeatedly  
> 🠊 `<PAIR>` The sync pair: its id, as list-sync-pairs prints it, its alias in the default sync pairs file, or its local directory  
> 🠊 `[PATH]` Only this path, relative to the root of the sync pair

> `pause-sync-pair <PAIR>`  
> Pause a sync pair: `sync` leaves it alone until it is resumed  
> 🠊 `<PAIR>` The sync pair: its id, as list-sync-pairs prints it, its alias in the default sync pairs file, or its local directory

> `resume-sync-pair <PAIR>`  
> Resume a paused sync pair; its next pass catches up on what changed meanwhile  
> 🠊 `<PAIR>` The sync pair: its id, as list-sync-pairs prints it, its alias in the default sync pairs file, or its local directory
